section_summary: This section consists of U.S. Embassy Tokyo's monthly political and economic reports on conditions in Japan for October 1935 (concluding pages), November 1935, December 1935, and January 1936 (opening pages), together with transmittal despatches and internal State Department memoranda. The documents record intense external developments, including Japanese military subversion and autonomy schemes in North China, violent Soviet-Manchukuoan border clashes near Pogranichnaya and Lake Buir, Japan's demand for naval parity and a common upper limit at the London Naval Conference, enforcement of the Petroleum Industry Law against foreign oil firms, and trade controversies with Canada, Germany, and Great Britain. Domestically, the reports highlight the suppression of the Minobe constitutional theory of the Emperor, the court-martial indictment and trial of Lieutenant Colonel Saburo Aizawa for the assassination of Lieutenant General Tetsuzan Nagata, reactionary plots against cabinet members, Finance Minister Takahashi's fiscal resistance to soaring military budgets, and the state-directed formation of the Domei Tsushinsha news agency.

subfiles.about: Concluding section of Embassy Tokyo's monthly political and economic report on conditions in Japan during October 1935, accompanied by lists of despatches and telegrams sent to Washington.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim
subfiles.summary: Contains the concluding portions of Report No. 109 covering October 1935, reporting on Japan's unified three-point program for North China and the visit of the Chinese Economic Mission led by Wu Ting-chang. It details armed border skirmishes between Soviet and Manchukuoan forces near Pogranichnaya, the reopening of the Manchuli conference with Outer Mongolia, Japan's conditioned response to British overtures concerning the London Naval Conference, and official Japanese attitudes toward sanctions in the Italo-Ethiopian War. Domestic political coverage includes the suicide of Conscription Section chief Colonel Chosaburo Yamada following General Nagata's murder, the Supreme Court's sentence reductions for civilian participants in the May 15, 1932 assassination of Premier Inukai, prefectural elections, Finance Minister Takahashi's efforts to curb the 1936-37 budget, and concluding monthly schedules of despatches and telegrams sent to the Department of State.
subfiles.title: Report on Conditions in Japan during the Month of October, 1935 (Report No. 109)

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing significant political, military, and economic highlights from Tokyo's monthly report for November 1935.
subfiles.summary: Summarizes Tokyo Despatch No. 1588 (Report No. 110 for November 1935) for State Department officials. Highlights the visit of a German economic mission negotiating Manchurian trade balances and soy bean purchases, the Italian Ambassador's submission of a protest against League sanctions, and the formal indictment of Lieutenant Colonel Saburo Aizawa for the assassination of Lieutenant General Nagata. It also notes police disruption of a reactionary assassination plot against cabinet members, the government chartering of the Domei Tsushinsha news agency to absorb Rengo, and cabinet approval of a ¥2,272,000,000 budget heavily dominated by army and navy appropriations.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 1588

subfiles.about: Embassy Tokyo Despatch No. 1588 transmitting monthly Report No. 110 on political, diplomatic, and economic conditions in Japan during November 1935, with lists of despatches and telegrams.
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, Chargé d'Affaires ad interim
subfiles.summary: Transmits Report No. 110 describing developments in November 1935, beginning with negotiations over the six-month oil storage obligations imposed on Standard and Shell under the Petroleum Industry Law and the inauguration of the Philippine Commonwealth. In external affairs, it analyzes the Japanese military's engineering of the North China autonomy movement, British inquiries regarding Nine-Power Treaty obligations, Japanese accusations surrounding British involvement in China's silver nationalization, the breakdown of the Manchuli conference with Outer Mongolia, and the departure of delegates to the London Naval Conference. Domestically, the report records the Grand Army Maneuvers in southern Kyushu, the indictment of Lieutenant Colonel Aizawa for the murder of General Nagata, the suppression of reactionary conspiracies, the establishment of the Education and Study Council following the Minobe controversy, the birth of a second Imperial Prince, and complete schedules of despatches and telegrams forwarded during the month.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1588: Report on Conditions in Japan for the Month of November, 1935 (Report No. 110)

subfiles.about: Embassy Tokyo despatch transmitting monthly Report No. 111 detailing internal political events, foreign relations, and economic conditions in Japan during December 1935.
subfiles.summary: Presents Embassy Report No. 111 covering December 1935, analyzing Japanese reactions to Secretary of State Hull's public statement on North China, ongoing corporate deadlock over the Petroleum Industry Law's storage mandate, and proposed protective legislation restricting foreign automobile manufacturers. In foreign relations, it traces the establishment of the Hopei-Chahar Political Council amidst Chinese student protests, renewed frontier combat between Soviet-Mongolian and Japanese-Manchukuoan forces near Lake Buir, Japan's uncompromising insistence on a common upper limit at the London Naval Conference, the settlement of the trade dispute with Canada, and the conclusion of the German Economic Mission's tour. Internal coverage reviews the opening of the 68th Diet session, Viscount Saito's appointment as Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal following Count Makino's resignation, the formal inauguration of Domei Tsushinsha, criminal investigations of the Omotokyo sect, and annual economic data indicating record foreign trade totals.
subfiles.title: Despatch Transmitting Report on Conditions in Japan during the Month of December, 1935 (Report No. 111)

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing significant political, military, party, and economic items in Tokyo's monthly report for January 1936.
subfiles.summary: Analyzes selected passages from Tokyo's monthly report for January 1936 (Despatch No. 1693). It notes Colonel Takashi Sakai's remarks disparaging Chiang Kai-shek's government as merely a local regime, the amity and currency treaty concluded between Manchukuo and the East Hopei autonomous government, and Premier Okada's New Year declaration affirming parliamentary government. It further examines the opening of Lieutenant Colonel Aizawa's court-martial trial, military agitation over the imperial polity controversy, political platforms in the general election featuring the rise of the proletarian Shakai Taishuto, and statistical notes on Japan's record 1935 foreign trade expansion and population increase.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 1693 (Monthly Report for January 1936)

subfiles.about: Brief State Department routing memorandum noting that Tokyo's monthly report for February 1936 focuses almost entirely on the February 26 military coup d'état.
subfiles.summary: A brief internal routing memorandum from W. T. Turner to Maxwell M. Hamilton and Eugene Dooman concerning the Tokyo Embassy's monthly report for February 1936. Turner advises that the report is largely devoted to the military coup d'état of February 26, 1936 (the February 26 Incident) and contains little new information that would warrant their close attention.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo's Monthly Report for February 1936

subfiles.about: Opening transmittal cover and table of contents of Embassy Tokyo Despatch No. 1693 transmitting Report No. 112 on conditions in Japan during January 1936.
subfiles.summary: Comprises the formal transmittal cover letter from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew forwarding Embassy Report No. 112 for the month of January 1936, together with the two-page Index and Summary. The summary outlines sections to follow, covering Japanese reactions to President Roosevelt's message to Congress, Philippine independence and textile quotas, automobile and petroleum legislation, relations with China, Soviet Russia, and Manchukuo, the collapse of Japanese participation in the London Naval Conference, cabinet developments, the army, and preparations for the national general election.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1693: Report on Conditions in Japan for the Month of January, 1936 (Report No. 112)
